This is the 1997 web essay, not the 1998 journal version. Its claims about professional secular history remain Chakrabarty’s argument, not a consensus or a characterization of all Indigenous historical practice.

Publisher-hosted primary introduction pp. 3–6 read: political modernity, useful yet insufficient European concepts, and explicit Fanon engagement. The excerpt comes from a later edition of the 2000 work; no later preface arguments are imported. Full book unread.

verification.note: Prior publisher check retained in history. Added primary preface xi–xv and title/imprint from publisher preview https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9780691188218_A33704825/preview-9780691188218_A33704825.pdf . Imprint states 1989 copyright and second printing/first paperback 2000; digital listing year is not original publication. Preface dated February 1988. Distinguishes culture’s logic from political-economic function, questions automatic capitalist homogenization, and advocates both equality and criticism of bourgeois individualism. Broad descriptions of Indian hierarchy remain the author’s contested claims. Book chapters, original mill records and Nair’s later-page examples not independently read; no whole-book or empirical adjudication.

verification.note: Primary scan pp. 82–87 visually read; scan heading identifies Oxford 1997. Participant criticism identifies changing emphases and internal tensions, while crediting empirical achievements. P. 83 supplies named Thompson reception and footnoted borrowing claims; Guha’s cited passages and the rest of Sarkar’s essay remain unread. Sarkar’s diagnosis is not a neutral consensus.

subaltern.label: Subaltern Studies
subaltern.description: Critiques colonial and elite nationalist histories; begins with subordinate groups’ politics and develops debates over representation and historical knowledge.
subaltern.representative_figures_and_works: Ranajit Guha; Shahid Amin; Dipesh Chakrabarty. Neither all South Asian history nor all postcolonial thought.

representative_people.context: Proposes an autonomous domain of popular politics while recognizing overlap with elites and variable regional social positions.
representative_people.works: “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India” (1982); Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983)

representative_people.context: Combines judicial archives and local interviews to examine peasant politics and competing national memories.
representative_people.works: Event, Metaphor, Memory: Chauri Chaura, 1922–1992 (1995)

representative_people.context: Revises universalizing class narratives through Bengal labor; later investigates historians’ translations of subordinate pasts.
representative_people.works: Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (1989); “Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts” (1997); Provincializing Europe (2000)

representative_people.context: Addresses the relationship between colonial nationalism and cultural difference within a changing collective.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

representative_people.context: Critically engages Guha’s autonomy claim and the gendered limits of recovering subaltern consciousness.
representative_people.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988)

representative_people.context: Historicizes communalism as a category and explores contested political communities.
representative_people.works: The Construction of Communalism in Colonial North India (1990)

representative_people.context: Examines science as both imperial authority and a resource for national emancipation.
representative_people.works: Another Reason: Science and the Imagination of Modern India (1999)

representative_people.context: Credits early research while contesting later priorities and identifying tensions within the initial project.
representative_people.works: “The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies,” in Writing Social History (1997)

representative_people.context: Recognizes Chakrabarty’s theoretical intervention while questioning static cultural categories and the treatment of gender.
representative_people.works: Review of Rethinking Working Class History (1990), 96–99

representative_people.context: Wrote the foreword to the 1988 Selected Subaltern Studies anthology edited by Guha and Spivak. This is a documented editorial contribution; it does not establish founding, collective membership or the direction of theoretical borrowing.
representative_people.works: Foreword to Selected Subaltern Studies (1988)

subaltern.scope_note: The collective changes across time; subordinate agency, colonial archives, and representation must not become a single unchanging postcolonial theory. Guha’s autonomy thesis, Spivak’s representation problem and Sarkar’s internal criticism are not interchangeable. Religion, gender, labor, local memory and colonial knowledge remain distinct questions; the present roster is geographically selective.

strands.title: Popular politics and elite historiography
strands.focus: Autonomy is an argued distinction, with interaction and regional variation built into the early statement.

strands.title: Local events, archives and remembrance

strands.title: Labor and historical difference
strands.focus: Bengal’s jute workers prompt criticism of universal class narratives that leave culture residual.

strands.title: Historical translation and its limits

strands.title: Nation, community and colonial categories
strands.focus: Nationalism and communalism receive distinct historical critiques; political communities are not timeless givens.
strands.works: The Nation and Its Fragments (1993); The Construction of Communalism (1990)

strands.title: Gender and the recovery of consciousness
strands.focus: Representation remains necessary and difficult; adding women to a list does not settle the problem.

strands.title: Science and national imagination
strands.focus: Scientific reason acquires different political uses under empire and nationalism.

strands.title: Disputing the project’s changing priorities

post.label: Postcolonial history / critique
post.date_label: 1970s roots · expansion from the 1980s · coverage through 2000
post.description: Questions imperial knowledge, Eurocentric universals, and the assumption that all societies follow Europe’s historical path.
post.representative_figures_and_works: Edward Said, Orientalism (1978); Gayatri Spivak (1988); Dipesh Chakrabarty, Provincializing Europe (2000). Gyan Prakash: “Writing Post-Orientalist Histories of the Third World” (1990); Stuart Hall: “When Was ‘the Post-colonial’?” (1996); Paul Gilroy: The Black Atlantic (1993).

representative_people.context: Studies imperial authority through texts and institutions, combining discourse analysis with hegemony and attention to particular writers.
representative_people.works: Orientalism (1978)

representative_people.context: Questions intellectual representation through colonialism, labor and gender; uses deconstruction critically.
representative_people.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988)

representative_people.context: Tests European social-science categories against South Asian political histories while retaining their critical uses.
representative_people.works: Provincializing Europe (2000)

representative_people.context: Develops colonial historical difference through an explicit disagreement with Anderson.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

representative_people.context: Examines ambivalence, mimicry and hybrid cultural production; these concepts are debated interpretations.
representative_people.works: The Location of Culture (1994)

representative_people.context: Criticizes homogenizing accounts of women and develops historically situated feminist solidarity.
representative_people.works: “Under Western Eyes” (1984; revised 1991)

representative_people.context: Reworks Foucault through colonial archives, race and sexuality.
representative_people.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995)

representative_people.context: Historical anthropology examines the colonial production of authoritative knowledge in British India.
representative_people.works: Colonialism and Its Forms of Knowledge (1996)

representative_people.context: His criticism of idealized and denigrating images of India supplies a specific resource for Guha’s environmental argument. Original article remains to be distinguished from its documented reception.
representative_people.works: “Orientalist Constructions of India” (1986), especially442, through Guha (1989)

representative_people.context: Historian whose essays set out postcolonial historiography from Indian historiography and read Subaltern Studies as postcolonial criticism. His Subaltern Studies context remains distinct.
representative_people.works: “Writing Post-Orientalist Histories of the Third World” (1990); “Subaltern Studies as Postcolonial Criticism” (1994)

representative_people.context: Cultural theorist whose essays on diasporic identity and on the category of the “post-colonial” are standard resources in postcolonial critique. His cultural-studies context remains separate.
representative_people.works: “Cultural Identity and Diaspora” (1990); “When Was ‘the Post-colonial’? Thinking at the Limit” (1996)

representative_people.context: The Black Atlantic criticizes national and racial closure and reads modernity through the Black Atlantic; a standard postcolonial and diaspora text for historians. His Atlantic and diaspora contexts remain.
representative_people.works: The Black Atlantic (1993)

representative_people.context: Coedited Tensions of Empire with Ann Laura Stoler (1997) and coauthored its opening research-agenda chapter. The publisher describes a historical and anthropological inquiry into relations between metropole and colony and changing categories of colonial rule. This contextual inclusion does not identify Cooper as an adherent of every postcolonial theory; his later criticisms require a separate dated claim.
representative_people.works: Tensions of Empire (1997), coedited with Ann Laura Stoler; opening chapter, “Between Metropole and Colony: Rethinking a Research Agenda”

post.scope_note: Said, Spivak, and Chakrabarty address different problems; literary critique and historical scholarship interact without becoming the same discipline. Feminist critiques, colonial archival research and theories of ambivalence introduce further disagreements. These selections do not make postcolonial thought synonymous with South Asian history, literary theory or all anti-colonial politics.

strands.title: Imperial knowledge and cultural authority
strands.focus: Texts acquire authority through institutions and citation; individual writers remain consequential.

strands.title: Representation and intellectual responsibility
strands.focus: Speaking for others and depicting them pose connected political problems.

strands.title: Provincializing historical categories
strands.focus: Critique works through inherited concepts without treating Europe as every society’s model.

strands.title: Colonial nationalism and difference
strands.focus: Bengal supplies the setting for a disputed account of cultural autonomy and political modernity.

strands.title: Mimicry, ambivalence and hybridity
strands.focus: Colonial authority and identification are examined through unstable cultural meanings.

strands.title: Feminist difference and coalition
strands.focus: Neither women’s situations nor feminist scholarship form a single homogeneous subject.

strands.title: Race, sexuality and colonial archives
strands.focus: Empire becomes part of the history of European bourgeois sexuality.
strands.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995)

strands.title: Critiquing the romanticized East
strands.focus: Guha applies Inden’s critique of hostile and admiring Orientalist images to environmental appropriations of Asian traditions. This documents a particular reception, without making those traditions homogeneous or certifying Inden’s whole argument.
strands.works: Inden (1986), quoted and discussed by Guha (1989),77–78/note9

strands.title: Metropole and colony in a shared research agenda
strands.focus: Cooper and Stoler’s 1997 edited collection supplies a contextual reading on connections between imperial centres and colonial settings and the historical formation of categories of rule. This is the publisher’s description and contents, not a passage-level check or a claim that one programme defines postcolonial history.
strands.works: Tensions of Empire (1997), especially the opening chapter credited to Stoler and Cooper

labourhistory.label: Labour history
labourhistory.date_label: Webbs 1894/1920 · Thompson 1963 · expanding comparative and feminist inquiries in the 1970s–1990s · coverage through 2000
labourhistory.description: Studies work, workers, labour relations and collective organisation across paid, unpaid, coerced, agricultural and industrial settings. Labour history includes unions and politics, workplace authority, household economies, culture, race, gender and colonial categories. Labour and labor are spelling variants; neither social history nor British Marxism exhausts the field.

labourhistory.scope_note: Institutional histories, Marxist cultural analysis, feminist inquiry and colonial labour studies coexist and disagree. Thompson’s work already contains a cultural reorientation; later gender analysis involves productive inheritance as well as criticism. This selection includes Britain, the United States, France, South Asia and Africa but does not constitute global coverage. Labour institutions and historical scholarship about them have different chronologies. Fuller Latin American, Caribbean, East Asian and Indigenous labour historiographies remain priorities.

strands.title: Unions, organisations and political institutions
strands.focus: The Webbs select a general union history from varied records, with Galton and union members contributing research.

strands.title: Class formation, culture and work discipline
strands.focus: The Thompsons and Hobsbawm connect political organisation with lived relations; culture is already internal to these inquiries.

strands.title: Workplace power and differentiated cultures
strands.focus: Gutman’s bounded population and Montgomery’s workplace/state inquiry reveal distinct US research choices.

strands.title: Strikes, serial research and workers’ voices
strands.focus: Perrot’s French strike research extends beyond counting events to gestures and testimony.

strands.title: Women’s work, gender and household economies
strands.focus: Alice Clark’s earlier research, Tilly/Scott’s work-family inquiry and Anna Clark’s gendered class history have different questions and evidence.

strands.title: Colonial labour, culture, caste and criticism
strands.focus: Kumar scrutinizes categories; Chakrabarty’s Bengal interpretation receives Nair’s criticism; Cooper studies African labour politics. These cases do not share one model.

strands.title: Workers as narrators and historical collaborators
strands.focus: Alice and Staughton Lynd’s editorial practice raises questions about testimony, selection and rank-and-file perspectives.

strands.title: Military labour and recruitment systems
strands.focus: Lucassen and Zürcher compare recruitment arrangements and household strategies without treating them as a universal sequence.
